h1: Buy grapes or grow your own: a new winery's first big choice
title: Buy Grapes or Grow Your Own Vines | Craft Beer School
desc: Compare buying grapes, contracting growers and planting your own vineyard: cost, control, risk and timing for a new winery.
teaser: Owning vines feels like the real thing. It also adds years of cost before the first sale.
standfirst: The fruit decision shapes your capital, your timeline and your wine. Here is how buying, contracting and growing compare for a new winery.
sections: You can buy grapes or juice on the market, contract specific growers to farm to your needs or plant and farm your own vineyard. Many wineries mix them, growing a core block and buying the rest.
Buying grapes and judging fruit quality

This is the fastest and cheapest way to a first vintage. You pay for fruit when you need it and carry no farming risk. In return you depend on the grower's practices, the weather in their area and a price that can rise.

Buy with a specification: variety, ripeness measured as sugar, acidity, a harvest date window and a delivery method. Take a sample from the vineyard before you agree. Good growers welcome tasting the fruit with you.

Wine can only be as good as the fruit that arrives. Sugar at picking sets the potential alcohol. Acidity sets balance and freshness. Sound, clean berries make clean wine, while rot or damage brings problems that a winemaker has to fight in the cellar.

Check fruit at the weighbridge or the crush pad before you accept it: look at it, taste it, measure sugar with a refractometer and note the temperature. Heat is a real issue in warm regions, since fruit picked and left in the sun starts to spoil. Many wineries pick at night or early morning for this reason.

A contract lets you specify yields, picking dates and vineyard practice. In return you share some of the vintage risk and commit to a longer relationship. Agree terms in writing: price basis, quality measures, what happens in a short crop and who pays for transport.

The grower must also earn a fair return or quality will drift.

Build two columns for the same five years. In one, buy fruit at a price you can document. In the other, plant, farm and wait. Include land, vines, trellis, water, labour, machinery and the cost of money. For each year, show cash out and bottles made. The comparison will not give a perfect answer but it shows where each route needs funding and when.

Add one test: what happens if a vintage is lost to weather or disease? Growers carry that loss directly. Buyers can look to another source, which is a real advantage of staying flexible early on.

Planting gives control over site, variety and viticulture plus a story customers like. It also takes land, water, labour, trellising and several seasons before vines give a useful crop. A vineyard is a farm business. The weather, pests and disease are yours to manage.

Site and variety must suit each other. In hotter, wetter or more humid regions, disease pressure and ripening patterns change what grows well. Get local viticulture advice before you plant.
Cash, timing and a staged path

Buying grapes puts the cost in the harvest season. Growing puts cost into land, planting and years of upkeep before any revenue. For a first-time founder, buying fruit for the first vintages while you learn, then planting if the business proves itself, often reduces risk. This is a general pattern, not a rule.

Work it out in your own cash flow. See boutique winery economics and why ageing ties up money.

Buying first, learning the style and the market, then contracting or planting once demand is proven is slower for the story. It is gentler on the bank balance. Whatever you choose, record the decision, the assumptions behind it and the point at which you would change course.

If you plan to apply for a loan, the lender will ask about fruit security. A signed supply agreement with a grower is stronger evidence than a verbal promise.

• Do you have suitable land and water?
  • Can you fund years of vineyard cost with no sales?
  • Do you have viticulture skill on the team?
  • Are there reliable growers nearby?
  • Does your brand story depend on estate fruit?

If the answers lean to no, buy first. If your whole concept is a place and a site, grow, but fund the wait.
faqs: Is it cheaper to buy grapes?
In the early years, usually yes, because you avoid land, planting and farm costs. Over the long term it depends on grape prices and your yields.
Can I make wine from table grapes?
You can, but wine grape varieties are chosen for sugar, acidity and flavour. Test the fruit and expect a different style.
How long does a new vineyard take to crop?
Several seasons before a useful harvest. Your viticulture adviser can give a local estimate.
Fruit wines use other fruit. See our guide on starting a fruit wine business.
